title: The enforcement discretion
paras: Start with the enforcement discretion. An authority can issue a notice where there appears to be a breach and it's expedient to act, weighing the development plan and other material considerations, but it's never obliged to, and national policy asks for a proportionate response. Expedient isn't convenient or politically comfortable; it means the action serves a real planning purpose, the harm justifies the resource, and the outcome is achievable. So run the public interest test: what harm is the breach causing, and does that justify acting?

Sometimes not acting is right. A well-designed marginal extension that harms nobody and would be granted on application draws a letter inviting a retrospective application; if none comes and there's no harm, record that action isn't expedient and close the file. But discretion isn't cover for inaction: unauthorised works to a listed building, a felled protected tree, harm to Green Belt openness, or a commercial use disturbing people day and night all demand prompt action.

Negotiation resolves most breaches, but only with discipline: a clear objective, a timetable, and the willingness to walk away when it stops delivering. A deadline you don't enforce isn't a deadline. And weigh the householder who genuinely didn't know against the developer running the clock on a twice-refused site.

However you decide, record it so a stranger could follow the reasoning: the breach, the harm or its absence, the policy position, the representations, and why action isn't expedient. "Not expedient" alone defends nothing at the ombudsman, who examines process, not merits. And be consistent, because declining on one extension sets a precedent, so a different view next time needs a recorded reason, underpinned by a clear policy and a prioritisation framework, high, medium, low, with response times you keep to.

title: Breach, immunity & evidence
paras: Now breach, immunity and evidence. A breach is development without permission, or breach of a condition or limitation, and neither is a crime, this is a civil regime, not a crime scene. But the exceptions matter as much: unauthorised works to a listed building are a crime the moment they're done, with no notice, no time limit and unlimited penalties; an advert without consent is an offence with a continuing daily element; works to a protected tree are an absolute offence, ignorance no defence; and ripping out a protected countryside hedgerow without notification is an offence that catches Class Q conversions. So categorise it first, civil or criminal, because that fixes the tools and the procedure.

Before reaching for any tool, prove there's a breach at all. Check the permitted development order first; if it's permitted development the investigation's over. Internal works, maintenance, moving within a use class, de minimis matters and agricultural use of land are not development. On a change of use, pin down the planning unit first, because a farm may be one unit or several and the wrong unit alleges the wrong breach on the wrong land. And keep lawfulness and permission separate: a use immune through passage of time is lawful by immunity, not approved, and a certificate of lawfulness only confirms the window has closed.

The time limits changed fundamentally in 2024, with a cut-off date in the written guide. A breach on or after it carries a single ten-year period, replacing the old four-year rule, but the transition leaves two tracks for years: operational development substantially completed before that cut-off, and changes of use to a single dwellinghouse before it, keep the four-year limit, and misjudging the split loses the out-of-time ground with no remedy. Substantially completed means capable of use for its purpose, not fully finished, so the clock runs while ancillary works are dragged out. And two things reopen a closed window: deliberate concealment, real steps to hide the breach, can disapply the limits through a magistrates' order within six months of knowing enough, and that order then opens a fresh year to enforce; and where a notice proves defective there's a second bite within four years of the previous action.

Investigation starts at a desk: planning history, previous enforcement, the land registry so you serve the right people, and historic mapping, where a photo of bare land defeats a claim of fifteen years' use. Then on site: date-stamped photographs, measurements, and signed notes of anything volunteered, when works started and who did them. And go past the obvious, because building control, licensing, environmental health, council tax and the electoral register often decide which time limit applies.

title: The Planning Contravention Notice
paras: Next, the planning contravention notice. You can serve it on an owner, occupier, or anyone with an interest in the land or carrying out operations, where a breach may have happened, the threshold deliberately low, may, not has. It's an investigative tool for when you need information, not a way of announcing conclusions in a case already made out. And it's discretionary: where the breach is obvious and delay would let it worsen or the clock run, going straight to a notice is proper.

It makes the recipient state what operations have been carried out, what the land's used for, and whether conditions are complied with, and can invite them to say how a breach might be resolved. They get 21 days. Not responding is a criminal offence, and so is a false or misleading answer, though that sanction is rarely used and a calculating recipient may say little or nothing.

It's not available for listed buildings, conservation areas, hazardous substances or trees, which carry their own investigative powers, and it can't compel self-incrimination where the conduct could be criminal, where the PACE framework governs instead. And unlike enforcement, stop and breach of condition notices, it isn't on the register, isn't a land charge, and doesn't bind a purchaser, so if the land changes hands mid-investigation, consider a fresh notice on the new owner.

It does its best work where a use's nature or history is unclear, where you need the extent of a condition breach, or where ownership is uncertain. It's least useful, sometimes counterproductive, against clearly visible unauthorised building work, which only alerts the recipient. But a signed response is evidence: one commencement date in the response and a different one at appeal is an inconsistency to explain.

title: Enforcement notices: drafting to survive
paras: Now enforcement notices, drafting them to survive. You need both a breach and the judgment that acting is expedient, properly authorised, usually under delegated powers on a report covering the breach, harm, merits and expediency, with committee sign-off where it's politically sensitive. The notice must spell out the land, on an Ordnance Survey plan edged red, because a verbal description invites argument about scope, then the matters constituting the breach, the steps required or activities to cease, the reasons it's expedient, and the effective date and compliance period. Get any wrong and you've handed over a ground of appeal.

The breach description is where most notices fail. It must be precise enough that the recipient knows what's alleged, accurate about what happened, and in plain English, because a prosecution can collapse if a court finds the notice incomprehensible to a lay person. And complete: in a mixed-use case, identify every use, because a complied-with notice deems permission granted for whatever it leaves standing, so allege only the vehicle-repair use on a site whose residential use was also unauthorised and you may deem permission for the use you'd have refused. Identify everything first, then decide deliberately what to allege and what to leave.

The requirements follow the Mansi principle: compliance must leave the land as it was before the breach, no better and, critically, no worse. Work out what was there before, what changed, and require precisely that difference; too loose and you over-enforce onto pre-existing development, and reinstatement beyond what the breach demands does the same in reverse. Deliberate under-enforcement is legitimate, removing the offending storey rather than the whole building, as long as the deemed-permission consequence is a recorded choice, not an accident. And the requirements must match the breach description exactly; a mismatch is the commonest avoidable drafting failure.

Compliance periods are tested against what a reasonable person needs: weeks for a small structure or clean cessation, months for substantial demolition or relocating a business, stepped periods where a use must stop fast but removal can follow. Service goes to the owner, occupier and anyone with a materially affected interest, known mortgagees included, not more than 28 days after issue and not less than 28 days before the effective date, with the note on appeal rights. Do the land registry search immediately before service. And an appeal lodged before the effective date suspends the notice until determined, so a robust notice, hard to appeal on drafting grounds, saves months.

title: Stop notices & urgent intervention
paras: Stop notices, and urgent intervention. A stop notice is an accelerant bolted onto an enforcement notice; it can't stand alone. It prohibits a specified activity within as little as three days of service, or immediately where you state special reasons with it, urgent environmental harm, irreversible heritage damage or public safety. It can't stop use of a building as a dwellinghouse, though it can stop use of land as a residential caravan site. Contravene one and it's an offence with an unlimited fine, the court required to have regard to the financial benefit gained.

The compensation risk is real but long overstated. It arises where the enforcement notice is quashed on grounds other than the merits, a technical or legal failure, or is varied or withdrawn other than on a grant of permission. Where an inspector quashes it by granting permission on the merits, compensation isn't automatic, and nothing's payable for activity that was itself a breach while the stop notice was in force. So an authority with its fundamentals right, a genuine breach, correct limits, proper service, is far less exposed; the real danger is fundamental error, stopping activity that was never a breach, was immune, or was defectively served.

The temporary stop notice is usually the more practical first response, freestanding with no prior enforcement notice, effective immediately on display, and since 2024 lasting 56 days rather than 28. But it's prohibitory only, it can't require demolition or reinstatement, and again it can't stop use of a building as a dwellinghouse. Compensation is narrow, only where an existing permission is complied with, permitted development, a later lawful development certificate, or withdrawal other than on a grant. You can't serve a second on the same activity without intervening enforcement action, so let one lapse without follow-through and you've lost the immediate route. There's now a listed building version too: suspect unauthorised works to a listed building and halting them for 56 days is the first tool to reach for.

Once the notices are served, upheld and ignored, three escalations remain. Prosecution for non-compliance carries an unlimited fine, the old twenty thousand pound magistrates' cap gone since 2015, financial benefit reflected in the penalty, and it's chargeable for successive periods, so a developer who carries on after conviction can be prosecuted again and again. Direct action lets you enter, do the required steps yourself, and recover the costs. And the injunction, the last resort in all but the most urgent cases, meets persistent deliberate defiance, irreversible harm in progress, or a breach you can see coming; breach it and you're in contempt of court, which carries imprisonment. Courts have generally not required undertakings in damages from authorities acting in the public interest.

title: Enforcement appeals: the grounds
paras: Finally, enforcement appeals, seven grounds. Ground A, permission ought to be granted, runs as a retrospective application on the planning merits, with a fee that lapses the ground if unpaid, and the 2024 changes trimmed its availability as a delaying tactic. Ground B, the alleged matters never happened, is a factual challenge met on the balance of probabilities. Ground C, the matters don't amount to a breach, is the legal challenge exposing a flawed categorisation. And Ground D, out of time, is now dominated by the 2024 transitional split, unanswerable if you got the limits wrong.

Ground E, defective service, isn't automatically fatal, correctable where no injustice results, but serious where someone with a material interest lost the chance to appeal. Ground F, requirements exceeding what's necessary, is Mansi territory where the inspector trims over-enforcement. And Ground G, compliance period too short, is the least contentious and readily granted. Anyone with an interest in the land, or any relevant occupier, can appeal, served or not, so investigate interests before serving. The appeal must be received before the notice takes effect, there's no discretion to accept a late one, and lodging it suspends both the notice and the compliance clock until determined.

Three procedures: written representations for straightforward cases, hearings where structured discussion helps, and inquiries for complex cases needing cross-examination, with the authority entitled to argue for the simpler route where the appellant asked for more than the case warrants. Your statement of case must address every ground raised, backed by the file. And the Inspectorate's timetable isn't optional: late submission can get evidence excluded, and serious delay can see the notice quashed for procedural failure alone. The inspector can dismiss, quash, correct misdescriptions where no injustice results, or vary the notice, but one so defective that fixing it would produce a substantially different notice can't be saved.

Costs follow unreasonable behaviour, not the result, and run both ways: against the authority for a notice unsustainable on the merits, resistance with no realistic prospect, or late or inadequate evidence, and against the appellant for unmeritorious grounds, failure to engage, or unreasonable delay. After the decision, if the appeal's dismissed the compliance period runs from the decision date, so diarise and monitor; if the notice is quashed, decide promptly whether a fresh one is possible, whether time's run, and whether the site has changed. And any challenge beyond the inspector lies only to the High Court, on a point of law, within 28 days.
